ex.am: State the electronegativity comparison explicitly before naming the bond type ('O is more electronegative than H, so the shared electrons are pulled toward O -- polar covalent, with delta-negative on O'), and when the item gives you experimental properties, let those properties decide the classification rather than the metal/nonmetal shortcut.
ex.core:
- Electrons are shared unequally, with greater inequality generally accompanying a larger electronegativity difference: bonding is one continuous scale from nonpolar to ionic.
- No cutoff separates the types; every polar bond has some ionic character.
- C-H, with a small real difference, is treated as effectively nonpolar.
ex.cpl: Treating ionic and covalent as two separate boxes, instead of a continuum where every polar bond already has some ionic character.
ex.hp:
1. Name the bond type.
2. Support it with an explicit electronegativity comparison: which atom pulls harder, which carries delta-negative.
3. Confirm with a property: conductivity when molten or dissolved, melting point, or brittleness versus malleability.
ex.pb: Back in practice, on every bond-classification item, write the electronegativity comparison down first -- then let its size, not the metal/nonmetal identity, decide where the bond sits on the continuum.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Compare electronegativities first, then name the bond type; given properties override the metal/nonmetal shortcut.
How points are lost: Treating ionic and covalent as two separate boxes instead of a continuum.
ex.title: Types of Chemical Bonds
ex.wsu:
- Metal/nonmetal is only a shortcut: use observed properties when they are given.
- Electronegativity predicts bond polarity, but molecular polarity (2.7) also needs geometry.
- For ionic attractions (2.2, 2.3) use the ions' actual charges and separation; metals differ because valence electrons are delocalized (2.4).

ex.am: When you rank two ionic compounds, name charge and ionic size in the same sentence and say which one dominates (for example MgO over NaCl because 2+/2- charges outweigh any size difference); when reading a PE curve, quote the x-value at the minimum as bond length and the well depth as bond energy rather than describing the curve's shape.
ex.core:
- On a potential energy vs internuclear distance graph, the minimum marks the equilibrium bond length; the well depth below the separated-atom baseline (zero) is the bond energy.
- Higher bond order gives a shorter bond and a larger bond energy together.
- For ion pairs, Coulomb's law ties strength to charge size and distance.
ex.cpl: Comparing only ion charges and ignoring ionic radius, or claiming a longer bond is somehow stronger.
ex.hp:
1. Read bond length from the minimum's x-value and bond energy from the well depth.
2. Rank length and energy together by bond order (shorter goes with larger energy).
3. For ions, cite both charge magnitude and internuclear distance, never one alone.
ex.pb: Return to practice and, on every PE-curve or bond-order comparison, state length and energy together as one bond-order consequence -- never rank one without checking the other agrees.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Say which of charge or size dominates; on a PE curve, the minimum's x-value is bond length and its depth is bond energy.
How points are lost: Comparing only ion charges and ignoring ionic radius, or calling a longer bond stronger.
ex.title: Intramolecular Force and Potential Energy
ex.wsu:
- This turns a bonding label into numbers you can rank and defend.
- It returns in lattice-energy comparisons, bond-length and bond-energy rankings in 2.7, and later bond-energy arguments in thermodynamics.
- It is one of the few Unit 2 ideas tested as graph reading.

ex.am: Explain ionic properties by the alternating-array arrangement and the many attractions it creates, not by memorizing lattice names -- the AP Exam explicitly does not assess knowledge of specific crystal structures, so naming a structure type earns nothing and is not expected of you.
ex.core:
- Cations and anions form one extended, repeating three-dimensional array that maximizes attraction and minimizes repulsion across the whole lattice.
- Properties follow from that alternating array, not from named crystal types, which the exam does not assess.
ex.cpl: Describing an ionic solid as separate molecules or discrete ion pairs, rather than one extended lattice of alternating charges.
ex.hp:
1. State that the solid is one extended, repeating array of alternating charges.
2. Link a named property to it. High melting point: many strong attractions throughout need a lot of energy to overcome. Brittleness: a shifted layer lines up like charges and repulsion cracks the crystal.
ex.pb: Go to practice and, on ionic-solid property questions, reach for the alternating-array-plus-Coulombic-forces explanation every time -- never spend words naming a specific lattice geometry.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Explain ionic properties by the alternating-array lattice and its many attractions; naming a crystal structure earns nothing.
How points are lost: Describing an ionic solid as separate molecules or discrete ion pairs instead of one extended lattice.
ex.title: Structure of Ionic Solids
ex.wsu:
- Hardness, brittleness, high melting point, and conduction only when molten or dissolved all trace back to this one picture.
- It links the Coulomb's-law reasoning of 2.2 to bulk properties in Unit 3, though its own exam weight is narrower than Lewis diagrams and VSEPR.

ex.am: Classify an alloy by comparing atomic radii out loud -- significantly different radii means the small atoms fill interstices (interstitial), comparable radii means one atom replaces another in lattice sites (substitutional) -- and cite the radius comparison as your reason, not the identity of the metals.
ex.core:
- A metal is a lattice of positive ions in a delocalized sea of valence electrons.
- Interstitial alloys (steel, small C atoms in iron's gaps) block sliding: harder and less malleable, yet still conducting.
- Substitutional alloys swap in atoms of similar size.
ex.cpl: Saying metals conduct because they 'have free electrons' without stating those delocalized electrons are mobile throughout the whole solid.
ex.hp:
1. Cite mobile delocalized electrons for conductivity.
2. Explain malleability: layers slide while the electron sea holds them together.
3. Classify an alloy by comparing the two atoms' radii: very different is interstitial, comparable is substitutional.
ex.pb: Head to practice and, on every alloy-classification item, compare the two elements' atomic radii out loud before naming interstitial or substitutional -- the radius comparison is the justification, not the alloy's name.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Classify an alloy by comparing atomic radii: very different means interstitial, comparable means substitutional.
How points are lost: Saying metals conduct because they "have free electrons" without stating those electrons are mobile throughout the solid.
ex.title: Structure of Metals and Alloys
ex.wsu:
- Delocalization from 2.1 now explains observable behavior: conductivity, malleability, luster.
- Atomic radius from Unit 1 tells the two alloy types apart; the size argument is a clean, frequently testable call.

ex.am: Write the valence-electron total as a number before you draw anything, then count the electrons in your finished picture and confirm the two match -- and for a polyatomic ion, adjust that total for the charge and put brackets with the charge around the final structure.
ex.core:
- A Lewis diagram is valence-electron bookkeeping done by a fixed procedure.
- Total the valence electrons: add one per unit of negative charge, subtract one per unit of positive.
- Place bonds and lone pairs to satisfy octets, converting a lone pair into an extra bond when a central atom is short.
ex.cpl: Drawing only the bonds and forgetting lone pairs, or ignoring an ion's charge when totaling valence electrons.
ex.hp:
1. The electron total matches the formula (charge-adjusted for ions).
2. Every bonding pair and lone pair is drawn, and octets are met where required.
3. An ion is bracketed with its charge outside.
ex.pb: Back to practice and, on every ion's Lewis diagram, write the charge adjustment as its own step before counting electrons -- add for anions, subtract for cations -- so the total you build from is already correct.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Write the valence-electron total first, draw the structure, then check the count matches; bracket a polyatomic ion with its charge.
How points are lost: Drawing only the bonds, forgetting lone pairs, or ignoring an ion's charge in the total.
ex.title: Lewis Diagrams
ex.wsu:
- The usual failure is the count, not the drawing: a missed ion charge or an undrawn lone pair changes the total.
- Every answer built on the diagram (resonance, formal charge, shape) inherits the error, so check the count against your picture first.

ex.am: Decide first whether your candidate structures are equivalent or nonequivalent: equivalent ones call for drawing the resonance set and describing an averaged structure, while nonequivalent ones call for showing the actual formal-charge arithmetic on the contested atoms and naming which structure wins and why.
ex.core:
- Formal charge = valence electrons minus lone-pair electrons minus half the bonding electrons.
- With octet requirements, it selects among nonequivalent Lewis structures; equivalent structures are averaged as resonance.
- The Lewis model cannot cleanly represent odd-electron species.
ex.cpl: Saying the molecule rapidly switches between resonance forms; it is one averaged structure, and the bonds are identical.
ex.hp:
1. Equivalent: draw all forms, reject switching, and state the real structure is one average (nitrite's N-O bond order is (1 + 2)/2 = 1.5, so both bonds are equal).
2. Nonequivalent: check octets, then compute formal charge.
3. Minimize formal charge, with negative on the more electronegative atom.
ex.pb: Return to practice and, before writing any resonance answer, decide equivalent-or-not first -- equivalent structures get an averaging statement, nonequivalent ones get real formal-charge arithmetic on the page.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Equivalent structures: draw the resonance set and describe one averaged structure. Nonequivalent: show the formal-charge arithmetic and explain why one wins.
How points are lost: Saying the molecule switches between resonance forms; it is one averaged structure with identical bonds.
ex.title: Resonance and Formal Charge
ex.wsu:
- Resonance forms are alternative drawings, not successive states: never say a double bond moves back and forth.
- That is why both N-O bonds in nitrite are identical.
- Formal charge picks which of several legal diagrams to reason from.

ex.am: Count regions of electron density first and count each multiple bond as a single region, then answer exactly what was asked -- a geometry name if the question says geometry, an sp/sp2/sp3 label if it says hybridization. Note the scope limit: hybridization labels stop at sp3, so for a central atom with more than four electron pairs give only the shape, and never reach for d-orbital hybridization or molecular orbital theory, which the exam does not assess.
ex.core:
- VSEPR counts regions of electron density (each lone pair or bond, however many lines, is one) to predict geometry, ideal angles and hybridization.
- Ideal angles: sp 180, sp2 120, sp3 109.5 degrees; actual bond angles can differ.
- Off the exam: deriving hybrid orbitals, d-orbital hybridization (over four regions: shape only), molecular orbital theory.
ex.cpl: Counting a C=O double bond as two regions and answering sp3; a double bond is one region, so that carbon is sp2.
ex.hp:
1. Count regions (a lone pair is one, a double or triple bond is one), name the geometry from atom positions only, and give the matching angle.
2. Assign sp, sp2 or sp3 from the same count only if asked.
3. For polarity, combine bond dipoles with the geometry to test whether they cancel.
ex.pb: In practice, count regions first, collapsing each double or triple bond to one, before assigning sp, sp2 or sp3; never use d-orbital or MO-theory language.
ex.qt:
The answer move: Count electron-density regions (a multiple bond counts once), then answer what was asked; hybridization stops at sp3, so give only the shape beyond four pairs.
How points are lost: Counting a C=O double bond as two regions and answering sp3; it is one region, so sp2.
ex.title: VSEPR and Hybridization
ex.wsu:
- Geometry is the payoff of the unit and the gateway to Unit 3: polarity, solubility and boiling point depend on shape plus bond dipoles.
- Hybridization identification scored a mean of only 0.56 of 1.0 on the 2025 free-response item, mainly from counting C=O as two regions.

ref.body: Covalent bond length depends on the size of the atoms' cores and on bond order, and bonds of higher order (single, double, triple) are shorter and have larger bond energies.
ref.title: Bond order, bond length, and bond energy

ref.body: When several valid Lewis diagrams are possible and they are not equivalent, use the octet rule and formal charge as the criteria to decide which one is the best model for predicting molecular structure and properties.
ref.title: Choosing among nonequivalent Lewis diagrams

ref.body: Metal–nonmetal bonds are generally ionic and nonmetal–nonmetal bonds are generally covalent, but electronegativity difference alone does not decide it, and the compound's properties are the best way to characterize the bonding.
ref.title: Classifying a bond as ionic or covalent

ref.body: Larger ion charges give stronger interactions, and smaller ions (shorter distance between the ion centers) give stronger interactions.

items.label: Larger charges
items.meaning: Interaction strength is proportional to the charge on each ion, so stronger.

items.label: Smaller ions
items.meaning: Interaction strength increases as the distance between nuclei decreases, so stronger.

ref.title: Coulomb's law and cation–anion interaction strength

ref.body: In a polar bond the more electronegative atom takes the partial negative charge, and in single bonds a greater electronegativity difference gives a greater bond dipole.
ref.title: Direction and size of a bond dipole

ref.body: Electronegativity of the representative elements increases from left to right across a period and decreases going down a group, which can be explained qualitatively with electronic structure, the shell model, and Coulomb's law.
ref.title: Electronegativity trends in the periodic table

ref.body: The Lewis structure model has limitations, particularly for species with an odd number of valence electrons.
ref.title: Limitation of the Lewis model

ref.body: Cations and anions sit in a systematic, periodic 3-D array that maximizes attractive forces and minimizes repulsive forces among the ions.
ref.title: Particulate model of an ionic solid

ref.body: In cases where more than one equivalent Lewis structure can be constructed, resonance must be included as a refinement to the Lewis structure. In many such cases that refinement is needed to provide qualitatively accurate predictions of molecular structure and properties.
ref.title: Resonance for equivalent Lewis structures

ref.body: Bond formation involves orbital overlap, and multiple bonds contain both sigma and pi bonds; sigma overlap is stronger, so sigma bonds have greater bond energy than pi bonds, and a pi bond prevents rotation about the bond and leads to geometric isomers.
ref.title: Sigma and pi bonds

ref.body: Graph of potential energy versus the distance between two atoms, used to describe the interaction between the atoms, with the lowest-energy point marking the equilibrium bond length and the bond energy read from the energy needed to separate the atoms.

items.label: Vertical axis: potential energy
items.meaning: Potential energy of the pair of interacting atoms.

items.label: Horizontal axis: internuclear distance
items.meaning: Distance between the nuclei of the two atoms.

items.label: Lowest point of the curve
items.meaning: Equilibrium bond length: the separation between atoms at which the potential energy is lowest.

items.label: Depth of the energy well
items.meaning: Bond energy: the energy required to separate the atoms.

items.label: Effect of bond order
items.meaning: Bonds with a higher order (single, double, triple) are shorter and have larger bond energies.

ref.title: Potential energy vs. internuclear distance graph

ref.body: A metallic solid is drawn as an array of positive metal ions surrounded by delocalized valence electrons.

items.label: Positive metal ions
items.meaning: Cores of the metal atoms arranged in an array.

items.label: Delocalized valence electrons
items.meaning: The "sea of electrons" surrounding the ions, not tied to any one atom.

ref.title: Sea-of-electrons model of metallic bonding

ref.body: FC = V - N - \frac{B}{2}

items.label: FC
items.meaning: formal charge of the atom (in units of elementary charge, e)

items.label: V
items.meaning: number of valence electrons in the free, neutral atom

items.label: N
items.meaning: number of nonbonding (lone-pair) electrons on the atom in the Lewis diagram

items.label: B
items.meaning: number of bonding electrons around the atom in the Lewis diagram (each shared pair counts 2, so B/2 is the number of bonds to the atom)

ref.title: Formal charge of an atom in a Lewis diagram

ref.body: The sp, sp2, and sp3 hybridization labels for a central atom correspond to ideal bond angles of 180°, 120°, and 109.5°.

ref.body: The established principles used to construct the Lewis diagram of a molecule or polyatomic ion.

items.label: Count every valence electron
items.meaning: The diagram shows all valence electrons of the species: the sum for its atoms, plus one for each unit of negative charge or minus one for each unit of positive charge.

items.label: Join atoms with shared pairs
items.meaning: Bonded atoms share electron pairs (single, double or triple bonds); the remaining valence electrons appear as lone pairs.

items.label: Use the octet rule where possible
items.meaning: Each atom is given an octet of electrons where the electron count allows it (hydrogen has two); the octet rule is also a criterion for choosing among valid Lewis diagrams (2.6.A.2).

items.label: Show the charge of an ion
items.meaning: The diagram of a polyatomic ion is enclosed in brackets with the overall charge written outside the brackets.

ref.title: Principles for constructing a Lewis diagram

ref.body: In a metallic solid, the valence electrons from the metal atoms are delocalized and not associated with any individual atom.
ref.title: Delocalized valence electrons (metallic solid)

ref.body: An interstitial alloy forms between atoms of significantly different radii, with the smaller atoms filling the interstitial spaces between the larger atoms (e.g., carbon in the interstices of iron in steel).
ref.title: Interstitial alloy

ref.body: A nonpolar covalent bond is formed when valence electrons are shared between atoms of similar electronegativity (e.g., C–H is effectively nonpolar).
ref.title: Nonpolar covalent bond

ref.body: A polar covalent bond is formed when valence electrons are shared between atoms of unequal electronegativity.
ref.title: Polar covalent bond

ref.body: A substitutional alloy forms between atoms of comparable radius, with one atom substituting for the other in the lattice (e.g., zinc substituting for copper in certain brasses).
ref.title: Substitutional alloy

ref.body: VSEPR theory uses the Coulombic repulsion between electrons to predict the arrangement of electron pairs around a central atom.
ref.title: VSEPR theory

w.q: Rank the C-H bond in methane, the O-H bond in water, and the Na-Cl bond in table salt from least to most ionic character, and justify the order using electronegativity difference.
w.strong:
| Bond | Electronegativities | Difference | Type |
| C-H | 2.55, 2.20 | about 0.35 | effectively nonpolar covalent |
| O-H | 3.44, 2.20 | about 1.24 | polar covalent, delta-negative on O |
| Na-Cl | 0.93, 3.16 | about 2.23 | ionic |

Na-Cl has the largest gap of the three, so it is classified ionic. Because ionic and covalent form a continuum rather than two boxes, even this bond retains some covalent character.
w.weak: C-H and O-H are both covalent bonds and NaCl is ionic, so C-H and O-H behave the same way and NaCl is a totally different kind of bond.

w.q: Carbon-carbon bonds get shorter and stronger as bond order rises: the C-C single bond is about 154 pm and 347 kJ/mol, the C=C double bond about 134 pm and 614 kJ/mol, and the C-triple-bond-C bond about 120 pm and 839 kJ/mol. Explain why bond order predicts both trends together.
w.strong:
| Bond | Length (pm) | Energy (kJ/mol) |
| C-C single | 154 | 347 |
| C=C double | 134 | 614 |
| C-C triple | 120 | 839 |

Each additional bond adds more shared electron density directly between the two nuclei, pulling them closer and deepening the well.

On the PE curve, higher bond order shifts the minimum to a shorter distance and makes it lower (more negative relative to the separated-atom baseline). Shorter length and larger energy rise together as one consequence of bond order, not two independent facts.
w.weak: The triple bond is strongest because it has three bonds instead of one, so there's more holding the atoms together.

w.q: Two students explain why NaCl is brittle. Student A says 'NaCl adopts a rock-salt (face-centered cubic) crystal structure, which makes it brittle.' Student B says 'shifting one layer of the lattice aligns like-charged ions, and the resulting repulsion fractures the crystal.' Which explanation earns credit on the AP Exam, and why?
w.strong:
Student B's explanation earns the point.

The AP Exam explicitly excludes knowledge of specific crystal structures: naming 'rock-salt' or 'face-centered cubic' is neither required nor sufficient.

Student B's reasoning is what the exam rewards: displacing one layer brings like-charged ions into alignment, the resulting Coulombic repulsion overcomes the lattice's attractive forces along that plane, and the crystal fractures rather than deforming the way a metal would.
w.weak: Student A's answer is more specific and names the actual crystal structure, so it should earn more credit than Student B's.

w.q: Steel forms when small carbon atoms occupy gaps in an iron lattice. Brass forms when zinc atoms (atomic radius comparable to copper's) replace copper atoms directly in the lattice. Classify each alloy as interstitial or substitutional, and justify the classification using atomic radius.
w.strong:
| Alloy | Radius comparison | Type | Second atom |
| Steel | carbon much smaller than iron | interstitial | in gaps between iron atoms |
| Brass | zinc comparable to copper | substitutional | replaces copper at lattice positions |

The types differ because classification rests on the radius comparison, not on both being metal mixtures.

Steel still conducts, since interstitial atoms block layer sliding but mobile delocalized electrons remain, although alloying can change its electrical resistance.
w.weak: Steel and brass are both alloys made of two metals mixed together, so they're the same type of alloy.

w.q: Draw the Lewis diagram for the carbonate ion, CO3^2-, and state the total number of valence electrons used.
w.strong:
| Source | Electrons |
| Carbon | 4 |
| Three oxygens, 6 each | 18 |
| 2- charge | 2 |
| Total | 24 |

With carbon central, one C=O and two C-O bonds use 8 electrons, leaving 16 as lone pairs: the double-bonded oxygen has 2 pairs and each single-bonded oxygen has 3. Every atom has an octet.

Enclose the diagram in brackets with 2- outside.
w.weak: Carbon has 4 valence electrons and each oxygen has 6, so 4 + 6 + 6 + 6 = 22 electrons total.

w.q: The nitrite ion, NO2^-, has two equivalent resonance structures: one with the N=O double bond on the left oxygen and a single bond to the right oxygen, and one with the reverse. Explain what the ion's real bonding looks like, and predict whether its two N-O bond lengths are equal or different.
w.strong:
The two resonance structures are equivalent, so the real ion is a single averaged structure, not one that switches between two forms. Each N-O bond has an intermediate bond order of 1.5 (halfway between a single and a double bond).

| N-O bond | Length (pm) |
| Typical N=O double | ~115 |
| Nitrite, both bonds | about 124 |
| Typical N-O single | ~140 |

Both nitrite bonds measure the same length, confirming the averaged picture rather than two different bond lengths.
w.weak: The ion rapidly flips back and forth between the two structures, so at any instant one N-O bond is a double bond and the other is a single bond.

w.q: Determine the hybridization of the central carbon atom in formaldehyde, H2C=O, where carbon is singly bonded to two hydrogens and doubly bonded to one oxygen.
w.strong:
Carbon has three regions: two C-H bonds and one C=O double bond, which counts as one.

Three regions means trigonal planar geometry, about 120 degrees, and sp2 hybridization, not sp3.

The costly error on the 2025 free-response item (mean 0.56 of 1.0) was counting C=O as two domains, giving four domains and sp3.
w.weak: Carbon is attached to four things -- two hydrogens, plus two separate bonds to oxygen -- so it has four electron domains and is sp3 hybridized.
